events.title: General Electric splits its shares
events.description: Each old share becomes two. The number of shares changes, but the split itself does not create a profit.

events.title: Apple splits its shares
events.description: Each old share becomes two. Doubling the share count is different from doubling the investment’s value.

events.title: The stock market crashes
events.description: Prices fall sharply on October 19. Heavy trading also creates serious problems in how markets operate.

events.title: The Fed offers support
events.description: The Federal Reserve says it is ready to provide money to help the financial system keep working after the crash.

events.title: Economists announce a recession
events.description: In April 1991, researchers say the economy stopped expanding in July 1990. The official judgment arrives months later.

what_happened_next.text:
January 1987 began with rising stock prices and worry about currency values. General Electric and Apple split their shares that year. Each old share became two shares, but the split alone did not add value to an investment.

In October 1987, the stock market crashed and trading was disrupted. In April 1991, a group that tracks the U.S. economy said a recession had begun in July 1990. The recession later ended in March 1991. The group did not announce that ending date until December 1992, after this story ends in January 1992.

IBM ended 1991 with a $2.8 billion loss after large charges and a shift in demand away from big central computers. GE reported first-quarter earnings growth in 1987, while Apple’s Macintosh II added color to its computer line. The three businesses had different challenges, and the same market years did not give them the same outcomes.

A company could remain important while its share price fell. Likewise, a market crash did not mean every investment would stay below its starting value forever. The amount invested, the type of holding and the dates all shaped the result.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: News included a rising stock market and worries about currencies. People also read about politics, winter weather, science, sports, and movies.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The crash and later recession changed the world investors faced, while each company and broad stock investment had its own path. No single event tells the whole story.
reflection.what_faded_away: The cold snap, Super Bowl preparations, and movie stories soon left the headlines. They mattered to people then, but they did not tell anyone what the next five years would bring.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: People in January 1987 could not see the October crash coming. They also did not know when the next recession would start or end, or how each company would recover. Later events did not make the future obvious at the start.

hot:1987-01:ibm.text: IBM recorded a $2.8 billion loss for 1991, including large charges for restructuring and job cuts, as buyers shifted toward networks of smaller computers. The loss and business shift marked a costly adjustment; IBM shares fell over this five-year window.

hot:1987-01:general-electric.text: General Electric reported first-quarter 1987 earnings up 16%, with stronger results in plastics, finance and aerospace. Gains across several lines helped lift the company’s results; GE shares finished higher over this five-year window.

hot:1987-01:apple.text: Apple introduced the Macintosh II on March 2, 1987, adding support for color displays to its Mac line. Customers could choose a Mac with color graphics; Apple shares rose over this five-year window.
